# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is written for the PhD student in computer science who has
discovered, often the hard way, that building a system is only half the work.
The other half is showing --- rigorously, defensibly, and reproducibly --- that
the system *does what you claim it does*, that the effect you observed is *not
just noise*, and that your results *generalize beyond the laptop on which they
were measured*.

Computer science has matured from a discipline where "it works on my machine"
was an acceptable result to one where empirical claims are scrutinized with
the same statistical rigor as in psychology, medicine, or physics. Top-tier
venues (SIGMETRICS, ICSE, OSDI, NeurIPS, CHI, MICRO) routinely expect
confidence intervals, effect sizes, significance tests, and pre-registered
protocols. Reviewers reject papers that report a single mean as if it were
the truth.

The goal of this book is to give you the conceptual vocabulary and the
practical tooling --- using **R** throughout --- to perform credible
quantitative research. We avoid the trap of "statistics as a cookbook."
Instead, each technique is motivated by a recurring CS research question:
How fast is my new algorithm? Does my compiler optimization help? Is the bug
rate of language A higher than language B? Does treatment X improve user task
completion?

All datasets in the examples are synthetic but realistic, and all code is
self-contained and runnable in a standard R installation.

## How to read this book

The early chapters (1--7) build the conceptual foundation: measurement,
description, distributions, intervals, and the logic of hypothesis testing.
Chapters 8--13 cover the workhorse techniques: comparing two or more
alternatives, non-parametric tests, contingency tables, and regression.
Chapters 14--19 are about *doing* research: planning sample sizes, designing
experiments, benchmarking systems, reproducibility, reporting, and avoiding
the pitfalls that get papers rejected. Chapter 20 is a reference appendix.

If you are in a hurry, read Chapters 6 (confidence intervals), 8 (comparing
two alternatives), 14 (effect sizes and power), 16 (benchmarking), and 19
(pitfalls). They will pay for themselves before your next submission deadline.
